en: The southwest monsoon, locally called Habagat, brings heavy rains to the Philippines between June and September.
Volcanic ash from Mayon Volcano enriches the soil in Albay, making it highly fertile for farming abaca plants.
Pumice is a light, porous volcanic rock that floats on water and is found in volcanic areas like Taal.
Cold temperatures in Baguio City cause water vapor in the air to condense into thick, observable fog.
The gravitational pull of the moon and sun creates the high and low tides observable at Manila Bay.
The Orion constellation, visible in the Philippine night sky from December to May, contains the bright red star Betelgeuse.
During a total lunar eclipse, the Earth blocks sunlight, causing the full moon to appear reddish brown.
A storm surge is a dangerous, observable rise in seawater level pushed ashore by strong typhoon winds.
The northeast monsoon, or Amihan, brings cool, dry air to the Philippines from November to February.
Cumulonimbus clouds are tall, dark, anvil-shaped clouds that observers see right before a heavy thunderstorm begins.
Quartz is a hard, glassy mineral that makes up most of the white sand found on Boracay beach.
Strong earthquakes can cause soil liquefaction, turning solid, water-saturated ground in coastal areas into a liquid-like mud.
